items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to translate and scale a circle given its equation in the coordinate plane.

Content:
For example, consider the equation
[MATH: (x-8)^2+(y-4)^2=36]
that represents circle [MATH: \text{T}.] Suppose that circle [MATH: \text{U}] is obtained by shifting circle [MATH: \text{T}] up [MATH: 3] units in the [MATH: xy]-plane. Let's find the equation for circle [MATH: \text{U}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d2076edb116d93e433d3009e03178e1d]

Content:
For each point on circle [MATH: \text{T},] we must add [MATH: 3] to each [MATH: y]-coordinate to get the corresponding point on circle [MATH: \text{U}.] So, the new [MATH: y]-coordinates of the points on circle [MATH: \text{U}] are given by
[MATH: y_{\textrm{new}} = y + 3.]
This equation is equivalent to
[MATH: y = y_{\textrm{new}} - 3.]
To get the equation of circle [MATH: \text{U},] we substitute this into the equation of circle [MATH: \text{T}.] Doing this, we get
[MATH: (x − 8)^{2} + (y − 4)^{2}|= 36; (x − 8)^{2} + ((y_{new} − 3) − 4)^{2}|= 36.]
Dropping the [MATH: \textrm{new}] suffix, we get
[MATH: (x-8)^2+\big((y-3)-4\big)^2 = 36.]
Finally, simplifying the expression, we have
[MATH: (x-8)^2+(y-7)^2 = 36,]
which is the equation of circle [MATH: \text{U}.]

items.title: Translating Circles

sections.normalized_html: The equation [MATH: (x-7)^2 + y^2 = 64] represents circle [MATH: \text{R}.] Circle [MATH: \text{S}] is obtained by shifting circle [MATH: \text{R}] down [MATH: 2] units and right [MATH: 1] unit in the [MATH: xy]-plane. What is the equation of the circle [MATH: \text{S}?]
sections.readable_text: The equation [MATH: (x-7)^2 + y^2 = 64] represents circle [MATH: \text{R}.] Circle [MATH: \text{S}] is obtained by shifting circle [MATH: \text{R}] down [MATH: 2] units and right [MATH: 1] unit in the [MATH: xy]-plane. What is the equation of the circle [MATH: \text{S}?]

sections.normalized_html:
We're given the equation of circle [MATH: \text{R}] [MATH: (x-7)^2 + y^2 = 64] and we wish to translate it by [MATH: 2] units down and [MATH: 1] unit right.

For each point on circle [MATH: \text{R}{:}]

  • We must subtract [MATH: 2] from each [MATH: y]-coordinate to get the corresponding point on circle [MATH: \text{S}.] So, the new [MATH: y]-coordinates of the points on circle [MATH: \text{S}] are given by [MATH: y_{\textrm{new}} = y - 2.] This equation is equivalent to [MATH: y = y_{\textrm{new}} + 2.]

  • We also must add [MATH: 1] to each [MATH: x]-coordinate to get the corresponding point on circle [MATH: \text{S}.] So, the new [MATH: x]-coordinates of the points on circle [MATH: \text{S}] are given by [MATH: x_{\textrm{new}} = x + 1.] This equation is equivalent to [MATH: x = x_{\textrm{new}} - 1.]

To get the equation of circle [MATH: \text{S},] we substitute the expressions for [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] into the equation of circle [MATH: \text{R}.] Doing this, we get [MATH: (x − 7)^{2} + y^{2}|= 64; ((x_{new} − 1) − 7)^{2} + (y_{new} + 2)^{2}|= 64.]

Dropping the [MATH: \textrm{new}] suffix, we get [MATH: (x - 8)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 64.] Finally, simplifying the expression, we have [MATH: (x - 8)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 64.]

Therefore, the equation of circle [MATH: \text{S}] is [MATH: (x - 8)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 64.]

sections.normalized_html:
We're given the equation of circle [MATH: \text{C}] [MATH: (x+3)^2+(y-2)^2=25] and we wish to translate it by [MATH: 4] units right and double its radius.

For circle [MATH: \text{C}{:}]

  • For each point on the circle, we must add [MATH: 4] to each [MATH: x]-coordinate to get the corresponding point on circle [MATH: \text{D}.] So, the new [MATH: x]-coordinates of the points on circle [MATH: \text{D}] are given by [MATH: x_{\textrm{new}} = x + 4.] This equation is equivalent to [MATH: x = x_{\textrm{new}} - 4.]

  • We also must double the radius of circle [MATH: \text{C}] to get the corresponding radius of circle [MATH: \text{D}.] The right-hand side of the equation of circle [MATH: \text{C}] represents the square of its radius: [MATH: r^2 = 25] Doubling the radius of circle [MATH: \text{C},] the new right-hand side of the equation of circle [MATH: \text{D}] must be [MATH: r_{new}|= 2r; r_{new}^{2}|= (2r)^{2}; = 4r^{2}; = 4 ⋅ 25; = 100.]

To get the equation of circle [MATH: \text{D},] we substitute into the equation of circle [MATH: \text{C}] and update the right-hand side accordingly to give the new squared radius. Doing so, we get

[MATH: ((x_{new} − 4) + 3)^{2} + (y − 2)^{2} = 100.]

Dropping the [MATH: \textrm{new}] suffix, we get [MATH: \big((x - 4)+3\big)^2+(y-2)^2=100.] Finally, simplifying the expression, we have [MATH: (x-1)^2+(y-2)^2=100.] Therefore, the equation of circle [MATH: \text{D}] is [MATH: (x-1)^2+(y-2)^2=100.]

sections.normalized_html:
The equation [MATH: (x+2)^2+y^2=36] represents circle [MATH: \text{R}.] Circle [MATH: \text{S}] is obtained by shifting circle [MATH: \text{R}] left [MATH: 2] units in the [MATH: xy]-plane. The point [MATH: (a,b)] lies on circle [MATH: \text{S}.] Which of the following is a possible value of [MATH: a?]

  1. [MATH: 3]

  2. [MATH: -10]

  3. [MATH: -8]

The point [MATH: (a,b)] lies on circle [MATH: \text{S}.] Which of the following is a possible value of [MATH: a?]

1. [MATH: 3]
2. [MATH: -10]
3. [MATH: -8]

sections.normalized_html:
We're given the equation of circle [MATH: \text{R}] [MATH: (x+2)^2+y^2=36] and we wish to translate it by [MATH: 2] units left.

For each point on circle [MATH: \text{R},] we must subtract [MATH: 2] from each [MATH: x]-coordinate to get the corresponding point on circle [MATH: \text{S}.] So, the new [MATH: x]-coordinates of the points on circle [MATH: \text{S}] are given by

[MATH: x_{\textrm{new}} = x - 2.]

This equation is equivalent to

[MATH: x = x_{\textrm{new}} + 2.]

To get the equation of circle [MATH: \text{S},] we substitute this into the equation of circle [MATH: \text{R}.] Doing this, we get

[MATH: (x + 2)^{2} + y^{2}|= 36; ((x_{new} + 2) + 2)^{2} + y^{2}|= 36.]

Dropping the [MATH: \textrm{new}] suffix, we get [MATH: ((x + 2)+2)^2+y^2 = 36.] Finally, simplifying the expression, we have [MATH: (x+4)^2+y^2 = 36.] Therefore, the equation of circle [MATH: \text{S}] is [MATH: (x+4)^2+y^2 = 36.]

Now, we need to find the range of possible values of [MATH: a,] where [MATH: (a,b)] is a point on the circle.

The center of circle [MATH: \text{S}] is [MATH: (-4,0)], and its radius is [MATH: r = 6.] Therefore, the range of [MATH: x]-values on the circle is [MATH: -4 - 6 \leq x \leq -4 + 6] which simplifies as [MATH: -10 \leq x \leq 2.] We can write this as [MATH: x\in [-10,2].]

Let's now consider each value in turn.

  • [MATH: a=3] is NOT possible since [MATH: 3\notin [-10,2]\quad{\color{red}{\times}}]

  • [MATH: a=-10] is possible since [MATH: -10\in [-10,2]\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

  • [MATH: a=-8] is possible since [MATH: -8\in [-10,2]\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

Therefore, the correct answer is, "II and III only."

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to translate and scale a circle given its equation in the coordinate plane.

Content:
For example, consider the equation
[MATH: (x-8)^2+(y-4)^2=36]
that represents circle [MATH: \text{T}.] Suppose that circle [MATH: \text{U}] is obtained by shifting circle [MATH: \text{T}] up [MATH: 3] units in the [MATH: xy]-plane. Let's find the equation for circle [MATH: \text{U}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d2076edb116d93e433d3009e03178e1d]

Content:
For each point on circle [MATH: \text{T},] we must add [MATH: 3] to each [MATH: y]-coordinate to get the corresponding point on circle [MATH: \text{U}.] So, the new [MATH: y]-coordinates of the points on circle [MATH: \text{U}] are given by
[MATH: y_{\textrm{new}} = y + 3.]
This equation is equivalent to
[MATH: y = y_{\textrm{new}} - 3.]
To get the equation of circle [MATH: \text{U},] we substitute this into the equation of circle [MATH: \text{T}.] Doing this, we get
[MATH: (x − 8)^{2} + (y − 4)^{2}|= 36; (x − 8)^{2} + ((y_{new} − 3) − 4)^{2}|= 36.]
Dropping the [MATH: \textrm{new}] suffix, we get
[MATH: (x-8)^2+\big((y-3)-4\big)^2 = 36.]
Finally, simplifying the expression, we have
[MATH: (x-8)^2+(y-7)^2 = 36,]
which is the equation of circle [MATH: \text{U}.]

Item 2 — Example: Translating Circles

Example Prompt:
The equation [MATH: (x-7)^2 + y^2 = 64] represents circle [MATH: \text{R}.] Circle [MATH: \text{S}] is obtained by shifting circle [MATH: \text{R}] down [MATH: 2] units and right [MATH: 1] unit in the [MATH: xy]-plane. What is the equation of the circle [MATH: \text{S}?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We're given the equation of circle [MATH: \text{R}]
[MATH: (x-7)^2 + y^2 = 64]
and we wish to translate it by [MATH: 2] units down and [MATH: 1] unit right.

For each point on circle [MATH: \text{R}{:}]

- We must subtract [MATH: 2] from each [MATH: y]-coordinate to get the corresponding point on circle [MATH: \text{S}.] So, the new [MATH: y]-coordinates of the points on circle [MATH: \text{S}] are given by
[MATH: y_{\textrm{new}} = y - 2.]
This equation is equivalent to
[MATH: y = y_{\textrm{new}} + 2.]
- We also must add [MATH: 1] to each [MATH: x]-coordinate to get the corresponding point on circle [MATH: \text{S}.] So, the new [MATH: x]-coordinates of the points on circle [MATH: \text{S}] are given by
[MATH: x_{\textrm{new}} = x + 1.]
This equation is equivalent to
[MATH: x = x_{\textrm{new}} - 1.]

To get the equation of circle [MATH: \text{S},] we substitute the expressions for [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] into the equation of circle [MATH: \text{R}.] Doing this, we get
[MATH: (x − 7)^{2} + y^{2}|= 64; ((x_{new} − 1) − 7)^{2} + (y_{new} + 2)^{2}|= 64.]

Dropping the [MATH: \textrm{new}] suffix, we get
[MATH: (x - 8)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 64.]
Finally, simplifying the expression, we have
[MATH: (x - 8)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 64.]

Therefore, the equation of circle [MATH: \text{S}] is [MATH: (x - 8)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 64.]

This equation is equivalent to

- We also must double the radius of circle [MATH: \text{C}] to get the corresponding radius of circle [MATH: \text{D}.] The right-hand side of the equation of circle [MATH: \text{C}] represents the square of its radius:
[MATH: r^2 = 25]
Doubling the radius of circle [MATH: \text{C},] the new right-hand side of the equation of circle [MATH: \text{D}] must be

Finally, simplifying the expression, we have
[MATH: (x-1)^2+(y-2)^2=100.]
Therefore, the equation of circle [MATH: \text{D}] is [MATH: (x-1)^2+(y-2)^2=100.]
